author: Song Yu-jeong
title: The Memory Bookshop
text:
Time seemed to stand still again. And then, finally: ‘Kim Jiwon-nim, the doctor will see you now.’

With difficulty, I got up, twisted the cold doorknob to the doctor’s room and pushed. The door opened with a creak, and I stepped through the frame into the yellow glow filtering from the inside.

‘Kim Jiwon-nim, what brings you here today?’

The doctor flicked his sharp eyes at me and threw out the banal question as he flipped a piece of paper over the plastic chart. I must’ve looked as stiff as a malfunctioning robot.

‘I …’

‘Yes, go on. What are your symptoms?’

‘I’m constantly feeling breathless and anxious, but I have no idea why.’

‘Have you been sleeping well?’

‘Not at all … I only manage to catch a few winks every night, and I also get sleep paralysis …’

‘Has anything happened or changed in your life recently? Something that might’ve triggered stress?’

The man, who looked well into his fifties, leant back against the plush leather chair. If not for his doctor’s gown embroidered with his name SPECIALIST SEO TAEHYUNG, he’d look no different from the average guy on the street. The doctor kept his eyes on the chart. Feeling my anxiety peak, I gripped my phone in my hand. How, and where did I start? I thought I was getting better, so why did the demons in my subconsciousness keep surfacing to destroy my life? I knew why. The reason was tattooed in the folds of my brain, but I couldn’t bring myself to talk about it.

‘…’

‘…’

A heavy silence wedged itself between us. At the thought of saying the words aloud, tears threatened to well up, and I struggled to keep them at bay. The doctor scrawled on the chart, looking obviously bored. He must’ve seen too many patients like me. I swallowed hard and moved my parched lips. The words tripped over one another as they tumbled out of my mouth.

‘Sometime back … my mum passed away.’

‘I see. How long has it been since her passing?’

‘Seven … years.’

‘Seven years?’

‘Yeah.’

The doctor shot me a look. I couldn’t quite read his expression, but it was somehow too much to bear, and I closed my eyes for a moment. I heard an incomprehensible sigh, and he started clicking his pen noisily.

‘I see it’s been quite a while.’

‘Quite a while …?’

‘Yeah. That’s what I said. Of course, we take time to process death. But seven years? You’ve been grieving for too long. You should be way past that stage by now.’

‘…’

‘Holding onto grief is not going to help you get better. You aren’t moving on.’

Grieving for too long … I pursed my lips, letting those words settle. Grieving for too long. Grieving for too long … No matter how I chewed over the doctor’s words, they didn’t make sense. I blinked slowly. A ridiculously long time to be sad over your mother’s death. The realization caught me in a chokehold, and I couldn’t even find the will to respond.

‘I’ll prescribe you a week’s worth of medication. Take it before bed. It contains sedatives, so avoid driving. We’ll monitor how things go after a week, and if the medicine doesn’t work, we can discuss your options.’

I pushed back the chair uncomfortably and stood up. Whatever feelings of nostalgia I had coming here were wiped away in an instant. This place was nothing but cold, hard reality.

Waves of regret washed in and crashed upon me.

I couldn’t write for days. And at night, my bed seemed to repel me, the terrifying darkness weighing down on me and forcing my breath to come in ragged gasps. I couldn’t sleep. The insomniac nights drew on, and I spent my waking hours in a daze, as though my soul was ripped from my body. Day melded into the night. Until sunrise and moonset, sleep evaded me. As the days stretched on, my head pounded as if it was on the verge of exploding. Bloodshot eyes stared back at me in the mirror. I was barely making it through each day.

Had I been suppressing too much? I’d never found it easy to be honest about my feelings. Maybe this was the so-called good-child syndrome. I’d wanted to be the kid who could keep their head down, do well by themselves, and I’d wanted my parents to be proud of me. Maybe that was the crux of my problems.

I turned on my laptop and stared at the white screen. Writing was my only talent – and also my livelihood – and it doubled as a way of confessing my innermost feelings. Right now, I needed to turn the painful lump in my chest into dark letters and expel them from my system.

Think. Come on, think!

I forced myself to focus on the blinking cursor as I tried to wring out some sentences. Lines of meaningless letters formed beneath my fingertips, only to be wiped clean as I hit the delete button. I’d started writing as a form of alleviation and release but now, it was only making me feel worthless. Frustrated sighs punctured my angry jabs across the keyboard.

The first word. The first sentence. The first paragraph. The first page. When it came to writing, the start was always the hardest. A good beginning is half the battle. Do up the first button right and everything will fall in place. Trite sayings, but true. Maybe things would become easier once I moved passed the beginning, but for the past month, I hadn’t been able to write a single word.

You’re too hard on yourself.

A voice flitted into my head, and I stiffened. Who told me this, and when? I couldn’t remember, but on second thoughts, everyone who knew me had probably said this at some point.

Don’t hole yourself away. Go out. Nothing like a good walk to boost your mood.

The voice nudged me to step out of my bedroom. Standing at the window of the living room, I stared out at the scenery drowned in a dreary grey light. Whipped bare by the chilly winds, emaciated tree branches swayed. It was a cold winter.
